correctness.rationale: For each voter and omitted candidate, SAV loses exactly \(1/|A_i|\) from baseline \(1\) precisely when the omitted candidate is approved, while PAV loses the same amount from baseline \(H_{|A_i|}\). Summing yields score vectors that differ by a committee-independent constant. The packaged exact-rational verifier checks the termwise identities and 57160 exhaustive small profiles.

evidence: Aziz et al. define SAV by \(\sum_i |W\cap A_i|/|A_i|\) and PAV by harmonic satisfaction \(\sum_i H_{|W\cap A_i|}\).
The same paper proves general PAV winner determination NP-hard and notes polynomial winner determination for SAV.
Brams and Kilgour introduce SAV as a distinct multiwinner approval rule based on fractional satisfaction.
broader_coverage.reasoning: This broader literature establishes that the rules are generally distinct and computationally different. General definitions and hardness do not imply that their complete objective orderings coincide on the codimension-one committee slice.

originality.rationale: The literature owns SAV, PAV, their formal score functions, and general PAV hardness. The inspected full text and targeted searches did not state the profile-independent one-vacancy equivalence or its minimum-normalized-support characterization.
residual_risks: A specialized handbook remark, exercise, software optimization, or unindexed note could contain the same one-vacancy simplification.

value.rationale: The theorem links two prominent approval-based committee rules that are generally different in both normative interpretation and computation. Electing all but one candidate is a natural nontrivial boundary case, and the exact collapse turns generally hard PAV winner determination into a simple normalized-support comparison while preserving the entire tie structure.
